title: Design a Feature Flag Service
summary: Millisecond flag evaluation on every request, globally consistent rollout percentages, and instant propagation — without a central bottleneck in every request's path.

slides.markdown:
The ask: turn a feature on or off, or roll it out to X% of users, without a redeploy. Every request checks a flag and gets an instant, consistent answer.

The trap in this design is treating flag evaluation like any other read — a network call per check. At fleet scale, that call happens on the hot path of nearly every request, so the entire design has to avoid a central service becoming a bottleneck (or a new point of failure) that every request depends on.

**Functional:** evaluate whether a feature is enabled for a given user/request, and let operators update flag configuration (percentage, targeting rules) without redeploying code.

**Non-functional:** **evaluation latency** that must not measurably slow the request it's checked in (sub-millisecond, ideally), **propagation delay** — how quickly a config change reaches every service instance — and support for **targeting rules** beyond a flat percentage (internal employees always see it, a specific country is excluded, and so on).

Evaluation latency is the requirement that eliminates the naive design outright: anything involving a network round-trip per flag check is too slow once it's on a hot path checked dozens of times per request.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: evaluations/sec vs a central service's capacity
slides.markdown:
At **50,000** requests/sec fleet-wide, and a typical request checking **5** flags along its path, that's `50,000 * 5 = 250,000` flag evaluations/sec. A central evaluation service, even a well-provisioned one, would need to sustain that entire load as pure added latency on every request — and any hiccup there now takes down every service checking a flag.

Compare that to local, in-process evaluation: 250,000 evaluations/sec spread across the fleet's own request-handling processes costs essentially nothing extra, because there's no network hop at all. The volume math is the argument for local evaluation, not just a nice-to-have.

Two operations, but with very different callers: `isEnabled(flagKey, userContext)` is called constantly, in-process, by application code on the hot path; `updateFlag(config)` is called rarely, by an operator through a dashboard or API, to change a flag's rollout percentage or targeting rules.

The asymmetry in call frequency is the whole design story: `isEnabled` needs to be nearly free, while `updateFlag` can afford to be comparatively expensive, since it fires orders of magnitude less often.

slides.sectionTitle: Stable bucketing: consistent hashing keeps a user in one bucket
slides.markdown:
A 30% rollout needs to put the *same* 30% of users in every evaluation, every time — otherwise a user would flicker between seeing the feature and not seeing it on every page load, which is a broken experience and makes A/B results meaningless. This is achieved by hashing `userId + flagKey` into a fixed range (say 0-99) and comparing against the rollout percentage — the same input always hashes to the same bucket.

Hashing in the flag key too, not just the user ID, matters: it means a user's bucket for flag A is independent of their bucket for flag B, so multiple simultaneous rollouts don't correlate with each other in ways that would skew results.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: hash-based bucketing for a percentage rollout
slides.markdown:
![A hash of userId+flagKey maps onto a 0-99 bucket range, split by a rollout cutoff at 30 into an in region and an out region](assets/hash-bucket-rollout.svg)

Raising the rollout from 30% to 50% only needs to move the cutoff line — every user already in the 0-29 buckets stays in, and new users only get added from the 30-49 range, never removed from what they already saw.

slides.sectionTitle: Local evaluation via a cached SDK config
slides.markdown:
Rather than calling a central service per check, each service instance runs an SDK that holds a **local, cached copy** of all flag configurations in memory. `isEnabled` becomes a pure in-process function call: look up the flag's config, hash the user, compare to the threshold — no network involved at all.

This is the mechanism that makes the latency requirement achievable: moving the cost from "a network round-trip on every check" to "an occasional background refresh of the cached config" is what turns 250,000 evaluations/sec from a scaling problem into a non-issue.

![Control plane pushes the source-of-truth config to many SDK instances via streaming or polling, each updating its own local cache](assets/config-propagation.svg)

Streaming push gets updates out in roughly a second; polling (say, every 10 seconds) is simpler to build but trades away propagation speed — the choice here directly answers the propagation-delay requirement from the NFRs.

assets.alt: Control plane pushes the source-of-truth config to many SDK instances via streaming or polling, each updating its own local cache

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: the control plane during a global config push
slides.markdown:
Local evaluation removes the bottleneck from the hot request path, but it reintroduces one at a different point: when an operator flips a flag, the control plane has to push that update out to every one of thousands of service instances at once. A global push during a large fleet's peak traffic is itself a burst of fan-out traffic the control plane must absorb.

The fix is treating this the same way a CDN treats cache invalidation — the control plane pushes to a smaller number of regional/edge relay nodes, which then fan out to the instances in their region, rather than one control plane holding a direct connection to every instance in the fleet.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: server-side evaluation vs client-side SDK evaluation
slides.markdown:
| | Server-side (central call) | Client-side SDK (local, cached) |
|---|---|---|
| Latency per check | A network round-trip, every time | Near-zero — in-process lookup |
| Failure mode | Central service outage blocks every flag check fleet-wide | A stale local cache during an outage — degrades gracefully to last-known config |
| Freshness | Always current | Only as fresh as the last propagated update |
| Fits | Low-volume, non-hot-path checks | High-volume, hot-path checks — the common case |

**How to decide:** client-side SDK evaluation is the default for anything on a request's hot path; central evaluation is reserved for the rare case where a flag genuinely needs to reflect state that can't be safely cached locally at all (e.g. a live incident kill-switch with zero propagation tolerance).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a synchronous network call on the hot request path
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Just call the flag service synchronously wherever we need to check a flag — it's a simple lookup."

**Why it's wrong:** on the hot request path, a flag check that requires a network round-trip adds real latency to every single request, multiplied by however many flags that request checks — and worse, it makes every request's success depend on the flag service's availability, turning a feature-toggle system into a new single point of failure for the entire platform.

**Correct model:** evaluate flags from a local, cached SDK config, never a synchronous network call in the request path. If a flag genuinely needs live server-side state, fetch and cache it asynchronously ahead of time — never block the request on it.
